claims.text: What the image looks like Pancreatic enlrg, peripancreatic fluid, fat stranding ± necrosis → acute pancreatitis (Balthazar grade)
claims.quote: Pancreatic enlargement, peripancreatic fluid, fat stranding ± necrosis Acute pancreatitis (Balthazar grade)

claims.text: Ex CT: a lrg acute necrotizing collection replacing most of the pancreatic tissue, < 4 wks after necrotizing pancreatitis first presented
claims.quote: This CT scan with IV and oral contrast shows a large acute necrotizing collection (arrows) replacing most of the pancreatic tissue < 4 weeks from initial presentation of necrotizing pancreatitis.

claims.text: Aspects (abnorm in red) Interstitial edematous: enlrg pancreas on imaging; peripancreatic stranding may be seen (a sign of inflam); most pts develop this type and the majority are self-limited. Necrotizing: pancreatic and/or peripancreatic necrosis, best seen on contrast-enhanced cross-sectional imaging; ≈ 5 to 10% of pts, w a prolonged, more severe course
claims.quote: Interstitial edematous pancreatitis is defined by the presence of an enlarged pancreas on imaging. Peripancreatic stranding may be seen and is a sign of inflammation. Most patients develop this type of pancreatitis. The majority of cases are self-limited. Necrotizing pancreatitis is defined by the presence of pancreatic and/or peripancreatic necrosis. It is best seen on contrast-enhanced cross-sectional imaging. Necrotizing pancreatitis occurs in approximately 5 to 10% of patients with acute pancreatitis and is associated with a prolonged and more severe disease course.

claims.text: CT w IV contrast = the imaging study of choice to diagnose acute pancreatitis and assess local comp; it = done early if the dx = uncertain or to exclude other Eti
claims.quote: CT with IV contrast is the imaging study of choice to establish the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis and to assess for local complications. It is performed early in the disease course if the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis is uncertain or to exclude other causes for the patient's symptoms.

claims.text: Later CT identifies comp such as necrosis, fluid collection or pseudocysts, particularly if abd Sx persist; necrotic pancreatic tissue does ⍉enhance after IV contrast; generally, MRI = preferred over CT for choledocholithiasis, pancreatic duct inj and necrosis
claims.quote: Also, once pancreatitis has been diagnosed, CT is performed later in the disease course to identify the complications of acute pancreatitis such as necrosis, fluid collection, or pseudocysts, particularly if abdominal symptoms persist. Necrotic pancreatic tissue does not enhance after IV contrast is given. Generally, MRI is preferred over CT for detecting choledocholithiasis and pancreatic duct injury and necrosis (2).

claims.text: CT severity index (Balthazar score): based on the degree of necrosis, inflam and fluid collections on CT
claims.quote: CT severity index (Balthazar score): This score is based on the degree of necrosis, inflammation, and the presence of fluid collections on CT.

claims.text: Dx needs ± 2 of: abd pain consistent w the dz; amylase and/or lipase > 3 × the ULN; characteristic findings on contrast-enhanced cross-sectional imaging
claims.quote: The diagnosis of acute pancreatitis is established by the presence of at least 2 of the following (1): Abdominal pain consistent with the disease Serum amylase and/or lipase > 3 times the upper limit of normal (normal range of amylase and lipase levels can differ depending on the assay used) Characteristic findings on contrast-enhanced cross-sectional imaging studies

claims.text: US if gallstone pancreatitis = sus (and another cause = ⍉obvious), to detect gallstones or a dilated CBD; pancreatic edema may be visible, but overlying gas frequently obscures the pancreas
claims.quote: Abdominal ultrasound should be performed if gallstone pancreatitis is suspected (and another cause is not obvious) to detect gallstones or dilation of the common bile duct, which indicates biliary tract obstruction. Edema of the pancreas may be visible, but overlying gas frequently obscures the pancreas.

claims.text: Plain films, if done, may show pancreatic duct calcifications (chronic pancreatitis), calcified gallstones, a “sentinel loop” (localized ileus of a small-bowel segment in the LUQ or center of the abd) or the colon cutoff sign in more severe dz; their routine value = unclear
claims.quote: If performed, plain radiographs of the abdomen may disclose calcifications within pancreatic ducts (evidence of prior inflammation and hence chronic pancreatitis), calcified gallstones, localized ileus of a segment of small intestine in the left upper quadrant or the center of the abdomen (a “sentinel loop”), or the colon cutoff sign (absence of air in left colonic flexure or descending colon) in more severe disease. However, the value of routine abdominal radiographs is unclear.

claims.text: CXR should be done and may show atelectasis or a pleural effusion (USU left-sided or bilat), signs of severe dz
claims.quote: Chest radiographs should be performed and may reveal atelectasis or a pleural effusion (usually left-sided or bilateral but rarely confined to the right pleural space), which are signs of severe disease.

claims.text: Eti Most cases are ← gallstones (40 to 70%) and EToH (25 to 35%)
claims.quote: Most cases of acute pancreatitis are due to gallstones (40 to 70%) and alcohol consumption (25 to 35%) (1).

claims.text: Gallstones: the precise mech = unclear but likely involves raised pancreatic duct P from obstruct @ the ampulla (a stone, or edema from a passing stone); ductal HTN → aberrant activate of digestive enzymes from acinar cells
claims.quote: The precise mechanism of gallstone pancreatitis is unclear but likely involves increased pressure in the pancreatic duct caused by obstruction at the ampulla secondary to a stone or edema caused by the passage of a stone (2). Ductal hypertension results in aberrant activation of digestive enzymes from acinar cells.

claims.text: Other Eti: mech/struct (gallstones, ERCP, trauma, pancreatic or periampullary CA, choledochal cyst, sphincter of Oddi stenosis, pancreas divisum) and met (hypertriglyceridemia, hypercalcemia incl hyperparathyroidism, estrogen use w ↑lipid levels)
claims.quote: Mechanical/structural | Gallstones, endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP), trauma, pancreatic cancer or periampullary cancer, choledochal cyst, sphincter of Oddi stenosis, pancreas divisum | Metabolic | Hypertriglyceridemia, hypercalcemia (including hyperparathyroidism), estrogen use associated with high lipid levels

claims.text: Meds: ACEis, asparaginase, azathioprine, furosemide, GLP-1 receptor agonists, 6-mercaptopurine, pentamidine, sulfa meds, valproate
claims.quote: Medications | ACE inhibitors, asparaginase, azathioprine, 2´,3´-dideoxyinosine, furosemide, GLP-1 receptor agonists, 6-mercaptopurine, pentamidine, sulfa medications, valproate

claims.text: Mech: an early event = intra-acinar activate of pancreatic enzymes (incl trypsin, phospholipase A2 and elastase), leading to autodigestive inj of the gland; the enzymes can damage tissue and activate complement and the inflam cascade, causing inflam and edema
claims.quote: Regardless of the etiology, an early event in the pathogenesis of acute pancreatitis is intra-acinar activation of pancreatic enzymes (including trypsin, phospholipase A2, and elastase), leading to the autodigestive injury of the gland itself (1). The enzymes can damage tissue and activate the complement system and the inflammatory cascade, producing cytokines and causing inflammation and edema.

claims.text: Sx Steady, boring upper abd pain (typically epigastric or LUQ), typically severe enough to need parenteral opioids, and it can radiate thru to the back; USU sudden in gallstone pancreatitis, over a few days in alcoholic pancreatitis; sitting up and leaning forward may reduce it; N/V are common
claims.quote: An acute pancreatitis attack causes steady, boring upper abdominal pain, typically severe enough to require parenteral opioids. The pain is typically in the epigastric region or left upper quadrant and can radiates through to the back. Pain usually develops suddenly in gallstone pancreatitis; in alcoholic pancreatitis, pain develops over a few days. The pain usually persists for several days. Sitting up and leaning forward may reduce pain, but coughing, vigorous movement, and deep breathing may accentuate it. Nausea and vomiting are common.

claims.text: Pts tend to appear acutely ill and sweaty; tachy, tachypnea and hypotension can occur in mod and severe cases; over 60% develop a fever
claims.quote: The patient tends to appear acutely ill and sweaty. Tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypotension can occur in moderate and severe cases. The lungs may have limited diaphragmatic excursion and evidence of atelectasis. Over 60% of patients develop a fever (1).

claims.text: Grey Turner sign (flank ecchymoses) and Cullen sign (umbilical ecchymoses) indicate extravasation of hemorrhagic exudate, occur in < 3% of cases and portend a poor prognosis
claims.quote: The Grey Turner sign (ecchymoses of the flanks) and the Cullen sign (ecchymoses of the umbilical region) indicate extravasation of hemorrhagic exudate, occur in < 3% of cases, and portend a poor prognosis (2).

claims.text: Tx and next step Her chart: aggressive IVF; NPO; address cause (gallstones / EToH)
claims.quote: Aggressive IVF; NPO; address cause (gallstones / alcohol)

claims.text: Basic tx: resuscitation w a mod fluid vol of lactated Ringer’s solution, analgesia and nutritional support
claims.quote: The basic treatment of acute pancreatitis includes: Resuscitation with moderate fluid volume of lactated Ringers solution Analgesia Nutritional support

claims.text: Start lactated Ringer’s @ 1.5 mL/kg/h; a 10 mL/kg bolus can be given for signs of hypovolemia unless cardiovasc, renal or other comorbid factors contraindicate it
claims.quote: Fluid resuscitation should be initiated with lactated Ringers solution at 1.5 mL/kg/h (1). In addition, fluid bolus of 10 mL/kg can be given if patients show signs of hypovolemia, unless contraindicated by cardiovascular, renal, or other related comorbid factors.

claims.text: Pain: parenteral opioids (eg, hydromorphone, morphine, fentanyl) in adequate doses; hydromorphone = USU preferred to morphine
claims.quote: Pain relief requires use of parenteral opioids such (eg, hydromorphone, morphine, fentanyl), which should be given in adequate doses (4). Because morphine can theoretically increase pressure in the sphincter of Oddi, hydromorphone is usually preferred to morphine.

claims.text: Early enteral nutrition = recommended (lower morbidity than delayed or ⍉nutrition); in mild pancreatitis, an oral low-residue, low-fat, soft diet can begin as soon as tolerated; enteral feeding = preferred over TPN
claims.quote: Early enteral nutrition is recommended because it is associated with lower morbidity compared to delayed or no nutrition (1). Patients with mild pancreatitis can begin an oral low-residue, low-fat, soft diet as soon as it can be tolerated. If oral nutrition cannot be initiated early in the disease course, enteral feeding is preferred over total parenteral nutrition because parenteral nutrition is associated with increased risk of infectious complications and organ failure.

claims.text: Prophylactic abx are ⍉recommended; start abx for an extrapancreatic infect (eg, cholangitis, PNA) or infected pancreatic necrosis
claims.quote: According to guidelines prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended in patients with acute pancreatitis, regardless of the type or disease severity (1, 5). However, antibiotics should be started if patients develop an extrapancreatic infection (eg, cholangitis, pneumonia, bloodstream infection, urinary tract infection) or infected pancreatic necrosis.

claims.text: Gallstone pancreatitis: most pts pass the stone spontaneously and do ⍉need ERCP; early ERCP w concurrent acute cholangitis; mild gallstone pancreatitis that improves → cholecystectomy b4 d/c
claims.quote: Most patients with gallstone pancreatitis pass the stone spontaneously and do not require endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP). Patients with acute pancreatitis and concurrent acute cholangitis should undergo early ERCP. Patients with mild gallstone pancreatitis who spontaneously improve should undergo cholecystectomy before discharge to prevent recurrent attacks.
